quickAnswer: Bolton is the least gas-served town on our list: utility gas heats only 54 occupied homes (2.9%), 50th of 50, while fuel oil heats 69.9%, 3rd-highest. A boiler replacement here often comes down to oil, propane or a heat pump.
body: ## Almost no gas, almost all oil

The Census Bureau's 2022 American Community Survey (ACS) counts 1,882 occupied homes in Bolton. Of those, 54 (2.9%) heat with utility gas, the lowest share of the 50 towns we serve, against 41.9% for the middle town. Fuel oil or kerosene heats 1,316 homes (69.9%), ranking 3rd of 50. Gas is simply not the usual alternative to oil in this town, since so few homes use it.

That makes the choice at replacement time fairly narrow: a new oil boiler or furnace, propane, or a heat pump. Oil equipment needs a yearly cleaning and tune-up. A heat pump heats and cools, and the electric utility's rebates may cover part of the cost. Whichever way a house goes, we assess its heating load before quoting, because a system sized from the old one can be too large or too small.
## Detached houses and very few renters

Single-family detached houses are 1,869 of the town's 2,005 housing units (93.2%), 3rd-highest of the 50 towns, and only 99 units (4.9%) are in multi-unit buildings, 47th of 50. Renters occupy 101 households (5.4%), 49th. The median value of owner-occupied homes is $679,600, 17th of 50, and the vacancy rate of 6.1% ranks 6th. With so few renters, the owner of each house is generally the one who decides on equipment.

The median Bolton home was built in 1985, newer than the 1975 of the middle town, and the town ranks 46th of 50 for oldest median year built. It still has a long history on top of that: 216 units (10.8%) date from 1939 or earlier. A house from the 1980s and one from the Federal period can need very different equipment decisions.
## A farm town on Route 117 and Interstate 495

Bolton lies about 25 miles west-northwest of downtown Boston along Interstate 495 and covers 20.0 square miles, nearly all of it land, and had 5,665 residents at the 2020 census. Wikipedia says the town is still home to many farms and apple orchards, the Nashoba Valley Winery and The International Golf Club, and it was incorporated on June 24, 1738. Wattaquadock Hill and Vaughn Hill's North Peak are the highest points.

Wikipedia lists several National Historic Places that bear on buildings. The Bolton Center Historic District includes civic, religious and commercial buildings along Route 117. The Pan Historic District holds a large collection of rural Federal style and colonial architecture. The Whitcomb Inn and Farm, from about 1708, is possibly the oldest surviving house in Bolton. Older buildings often have uneven insulation and little room for new equipment, so a historic house deserves a careful look before any equipment is chosen.
## Rivers, parks and the town line

Bolton seceded from Lancaster along the Still River, and the Bolton Flats Wildlife Management Area lies largely within town near the Nashua and Still Rivers. The town also has many other parks and conservation areas. None of that says how any one house is built, so the fuel, the age of the equipment and the insulation have to be looked at house by house.
## National Grid and Mass Save

National Grid's Massachusetts Electric Company territory list includes Bolton. Mass Save heat pump rebates therefore generally apply to Bolton customers, subject to program terms. The rebate numbers and conditions sit on the [heat pump page](/cities/bolton/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).

faq.q: Is natural gas an option for my Bolton house?
faq.a: For most homes it does not look like it. Only 54 occupied homes (2.9%) heat with utility gas, the lowest share of the 50 towns. Ask the gas company whether a main runs past your street. If not, the usual choices are oil, propane or a heat pump.

faq.q: Is it worth moving from oil to a heat pump in Bolton?
faq.a: It depends on the house. With 69.9% of Bolton homes on oil, many owners are comparing the two. A heat pump heats and cools, and a Mass Save rebate may help if the home is weatherized. Both quotes start from the same heating load assessment, so the comparison is fair.

faq.q: My Bolton house is a historic one. Does that change the work?
faq.a: It can. Older buildings may have less insulation, uneven rooms and little space for equipment or ductwork, so the equipment choice deserves care. A ductless system can suit a house where running ducts would be hard. Correct sizing matters more than the brand.

faq.q: Who can install a propane or gas boiler in Bolton?
faq.a: In Massachusetts only a licensed plumber or gas fitter may pull a gas permit, and a new gas furnace or boiler normally ends with a final inspection. The town's building department can explain the local steps, and your contractor should say who is filing.

body: ## The fuel mix beyond oil

According to the ACS 2022, electricity heats 263 Bolton homes (14.0%), ranking 16th of 50. Bottled or tank gas heats 183 (9.7%), ranking 6th, and wood heats 40 (2.1%). Another 26 homes use some other fuel or coal. Each fuel has its own logistics, and a replacement is a chance to decide whether the same fuel still makes sense.
## Propane and permits

A propane boiler or furnace counts as a gas appliance, so a new one normally brings a permit and a final inspection. Massachusetts reserves gas permits for licensed plumbers and gas fitters. Ask the installer who files the permit, and ask the town's building department about tanks and venting.
## Houses from 1960 to 1979

The ACS counts 588 Bolton housing units (29.3%) built between 1960 and 1979, and 99 more (4.9%) from 1940 to 1959. A boiler or furnace in a house that old may already be a replacement for the original. Leaks, rust or a noisy burner can mean the end is near, and when a repair bill is large it is worth setting it against the cost of new equipment.
## Wood and electric as the second source

Wood is the main fuel in 40 homes and electricity in 263. A wood stove or electric baseboard can be paired with a heat pump or a small boiler, depending on the house, the chimney and the electrical service. Bring those details to the estimate.
## Winter and repairs

A no-heat failure is urgent in January. Heating work covers installation and repair for homes and businesses, and a free written estimate comes before any work starts. If a heat pump is on your mind, see the [heat pump page](/cities/bolton/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).

faq.q: What if my Bolton house heats with wood?
faq.a: Wood is the main fuel in 40 occupied homes (2.1%), a small group but a real one. A wood stove as the only heat can leave a cold house when nobody is there to feed it, so some owners add a heat pump or a boiler. The right pairing depends on the house, the chimney and the electrical service.

faq.q: Who do I call for an emergency heating failure in Bolton?
faq.a: Call (508) 786-8755 at any hour, because Mass HVAC takes emergency calls 24/7. Say which fuel the house uses, roughly how old the system is and what you noticed, such as no heat, a smell near the burner or a tripped breaker. With 69.9% of homes in town on oil, the tank level is worth checking first.

faq.q: Is propane a sensible alternative to oil in Bolton?
faq.a: Propane heats 183 Bolton homes (9.7%), the 6th highest share of the 50 towns, so it is a familiar choice here. It needs a tank, deliveries and a gas permit for new equipment. Fuel prices change, so compare propane, oil and a heat pump on the cost to run, not only the price of the equipment.

air-conditioning-installation-repair.quickAnswer: With 93.2% of Bolton housing units detached, cooling jobs are mostly single houses rather than shared buildings. The median build year is 1985, so ducted systems and ductless mini-splits can both be worth a look.
body: ## One house, one cooling plan

The ACS 2022 shows 1,869 single-family detached units in Bolton (93.2%), and only 65 units (3.2%) in buildings of five or more. Detached houses give a lot of freedom about where an outdoor condenser goes, since there is generally no neighbor's wall or shared roof to consider. That is a general point, not a statement about each lot, and noise and clearance still matter.
## Ducted or ductless

A town with a median build year of 1985 has houses from before and after the spread of central air. Many older homes were built without it, and a house that was never ducted can be cooled with ductless heads instead of new duct runs. Houses from 2000 on, which are 482 units (24.0%) in town, may be more likely to have ducts already. Only a look at the house settles it.

A ducted system sends cool air from a central unit through duct runs. A ductless mini-split serves one zone per indoor head, which can fit a finished attic, an addition or a far bedroom. Mini-splits also heat, which ties into the [heat pump page](/cities/bolton/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).
## Cooling an addition or a single room
Some owners want to cool only a bedroom, an office or a new addition. A single-zone mini-split can do that without touching the rest of the house, and more heads can sometimes be added later.
## Sizing and humidity

Oversizing is the common mistake: a big unit cools fast, stops, and leaves the air damp. An undersized one labors all afternoon. Insulation, sun and window area decide the right size. Air conditioning work covers homes and businesses, both new installations and repairs.

faq.q: Can I cool a Bolton house that has no ducts?
faq.a: Yes. A mini-split connects each indoor head to the outdoor unit through a small wall opening and a refrigerant line, and the room layout decides how many heads you need. A house that was never ducted can skip new duct runs entirely, and each head can be controlled on its own, so an unused room need not be cooled.

faq.q: Would a mini-split suit an old farmhouse?
faq.a: Where ducts would mean opening walls, a mini-split is often worth pricing first. The Pan Historic District, per Wikipedia, holds rural Federal style and colonial houses. In a frame that old there may be little space for duct runs, and cutting into plaster or framing to add them can be a lot of work.

faq.q: Does multi-unit housing matter for cooling in Bolton?
faq.a: Only 4.9% of Bolton housing units sit in multi-unit buildings, so shared-roof and shared-wall questions are less likely to come up than in a town of condos. For most owners cooling means a system for a detached house, with the outdoor condenser placed on the owner's own lot and the choice of ducted or ductless left to the house itself.

body: ## National Grid territory

National Grid's Massachusetts Electric Company territory list names Bolton, so Mass Save heat pump incentives generally open to local customers. For 2026 the whole-home air source rebate pays $2,650 a ton to a cap of $8,500, and weatherization comes first. The full conditions are on the [main heat pump page](/services/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits), and they can change, so confirm at masssave.com.
## The weatherization test against Bolton's housing

Building date is the simplest way through that test: a house from 2000 or later qualifies on age alone. In Bolton that is 482 housing units (24.0%), including 203 (10.1%) built since 2010, against 8.4% for the middle town. The other 903 units (45.0%) predate 1980, compared with 57.2% in the middle town, and the 620 units (30.9%) from 1980 to 1999 do not pass on age alone, so an assessment would be the next step for them.
## What replaces an oil boiler

Oil heats 1,316 occupied homes (69.9%), propane 183 (9.7%), electricity 263 (14.0%) and utility gas just 54 (2.9%). For the oil group, a heat pump is one of the few options that needs no fuel tank. Propane and electric-baseboard homes may weigh a heat pump against what they run now.
## Where ductless fits

Of 2,005 housing units, 1,869 are single-family detached. Houses without ducts can use a ductless mini-split, with one indoor head per room or zone. Sizing starts from the heating load, which we assess before quoting a system.
## Cold weather

Modern heat pumps are designed to heat in cold weather, and the result depends on the house and the equipment. Bolton has 263 homes (14.0%) that already heat with electricity, a different starting point from an oil or propane house. The [Bolton overview](/cities/bolton) has the fuel numbers in full.

faq.q: Does Bolton qualify for Mass Save heat pump rebates?
faq.a: Bolton is on National Grid's territory list, so the rebates generally apply, subject to program terms that can change. Check masssave.com for the current conditions, and confirm that your installer is on the eligible Mass Save heat pump installer list before you sign anything.

faq.q: Would a house built from 1980 to 1999 pass the weatherization test?
faq.a: Not on age alone, because the test favors homes built in 2000 or later. Bolton has 620 units (30.9%) from 1980 to 1999, so a Home Energy Assessment, or completed recommendations from 2013 or later, would decide it. A house from that period is not automatically ruled out.

faq.q: Can a heat pump work through a Bolton winter?
faq.a: Modern heat pumps are designed to heat in cold weather, but results depend on the house and the equipment. With oil serving 69.9% of Bolton homes, many owners ask this before leaving a boiler behind. A heating load assessment sets the size, and a backup source is sometimes kept for the coldest days.

hvac-maintenance-tune-ups.quickAnswer: In Bolton, 94.6% of households own their homes and oil is the leading fuel, so a yearly oil cleaning, plus a look at older equipment, is the core of a tune-up here. Owners decide when to service.
body: ## Who services the equipment

The ACS 2022 counts 1,781 owner-occupied Bolton households (94.6%) and 101 renter-occupied ones, so most service decisions sit with the household that owns the house. A simple calendar helps: heating before the first cold weather, cooling before the first hot spell, and a call at any time if something changes.
## Matching the visit to the fuel

- **Oil:** burner and heat exchanger cleaned, filter and nozzle replaced, combustion checked, once a year.
- **Propane:** burner, venting and controls checked for safety and efficiency.
- **Heat pump or mini-split:** filters and coils cleaned, refrigerant side inspected.
- **Wood:** chimney and flue looked at before the season.
Exact steps depend on the equipment and its age.
## A median house from 1985

Bolton's median year built is 1985, ten years newer than the 1975 of the middle town. If a boiler or furnace is original to a house of that vintage, it is already a long-lived unit, and a service record helps decide when to repair and when to replace. Keep a note of each visit, with the date and what was changed.
## Older buildings

Bolton has 216 housing units (10.8%) built in 1939 or earlier. In an old house a tune-up can show whether the boiler is working harder than it should. Leaks, rust, short cycling and rising fuel use are signs of wear, and noticing them early may let you plan a replacement instead of facing a failure in January.
## Cooling equipment too

A central air conditioner or mini-split also benefits from a yearly look: clean coils, a clear drain line and a free-spinning fan are the basics. Outdoor units need room around them, free of leaves, snow and shrubs. A spring visit means the system is ready before the first hot weekend.
## Before the visit

Write down the fuel, the rough age of the equipment and anything unusual you have heard or smelled. Mass HVAC offers maintenance for homes and businesses. For repairs and replacements, see the [heating page](/cities/bolton/heating-installation-repair).

faq.q: How often should an oil boiler in Bolton be cleaned?
faq.a: Once a year, ideally before the heating season starts. Oil heats 1,316 occupied homes in town, so this is a common job. A yearly visit keeps the burner running cleanly and can catch a worn nozzle or a dirty filter before a cold night exposes it.

faq.q: Is a tune-up worth it on a newer system?
faq.a: Usually. Even newer equipment benefits from clean filters, coils and burners, and a visit can catch an early fault while it is still cheap to fix. It also gives you a baseline, so changes in noise, smell or running time stand out in later years.

faq.q: When should I schedule a cooling tune-up in Bolton?
faq.a: Spring, before the first hot weekend, is the usual choice for central air and mini-splits. Heat pumps do both jobs, so they benefit from a look before each season. Booking heating and cooling work at different times of year keeps either system from being forgotten.

indoor-air-quality.quickAnswer: In Bolton, 30.9% of homes were built from 1980 to 1999, a period of tighter construction than the oldest houses. Tighter homes may need ventilation, older ones leak air, and filters and humidity matter in both.
body: ## Houses of different ages

According to the ACS 2022, 620 Bolton housing units (30.9%) date from 1980 to 1999, the largest age band in town. Houses from that period are often tighter than older ones, and a tight house can hold moisture and odors longer. Mechanical ventilation can help. The oldest houses often leak more air, bringing in outdoor air together with dust, pollen and humidity.
## Combustion and wood

Oil leads the heating mix in Bolton, with bottled gas and wood behind it. Burning fuels give off combustion gases, so a yearly check of the chimney, flue and burner and a working carbon monoxide alarm are the basics. Soot or a smell near the burner is a reason to call.
## A stuffy room or a musty smell

Complaints usually start small: a room that feels close, dust that returns within days, condensation on windows. Each points toward a different cause, from a clogged filter to excess moisture to too little fresh air. Naming the room and the time of year narrows it down quickly.
## Shared walls and small buildings

Bolton counts 37 attached townhouse units (1.8%) and 26 housing units in two-unit buildings (1.3%). Where walls and floors are shared, cooking smells and smoke can travel between units, so a bathroom or kitchen exhaust fan that vents outside matters more there than in a detached house.
## Reading the house

Three details usually narrow the options: when the house was built, whether it has ducts and where the problem shows up. Those answers often point to a filter, a humidity control or a fan as the sensible first step.
## Choices for the house

Filtration, humidity control, exhaust fans and whole-house ventilation each fit a different problem. A higher-rated filter is not always an improvement if the blower struggles with it. Duct cleaning helps only where the ducts are actually dirty or damaged.

Mass HVAC does indoor air quality work for homes and businesses. Not every problem needs equipment, and a filter or a fan is sometimes enough. See the [Bolton page](/cities/bolton) for the town overview.

faq.q: Does a house built from 1980 to 1999 need ventilation?
faq.a: It may benefit, because tighter construction can hold moisture and odors. Which equipment helps depends on how the house is built and used.

faq.q: When does duct cleaning make sense in Bolton?
faq.a: When ducts are visibly dirty, damaged or exposed to renovation dust. If they are in good shape, regular filter changes may be enough.

faq.q: Do wood stoves affect indoor air in a Bolton house?
faq.a: They can. Wood heats 40 occupied homes in town (2.1%), and smoke or ash can escape when a stove door is opened or a flue draws poorly. A clean, inspected chimney, a working carbon monoxide alarm and a dry fuel supply cut the risk, and an exhaust fan can pull air the wrong way if the house is tight.
